To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the cyanovinyloxy moiety of TMC278 occupies a hydrophobic pocket that extends from the NNRTI-binding pocket to the nucleotide binding site, and that this pocket has the capacity to change its conformation to accommodate the inhibitor and the resistance mutations, which is the basis for the potent activity of TMC278 against drug resistant HIV  1.
TMC278 binds to HIV-1 RT in a hydrophobically shaped tunnel, and that the drug adapts to the binding pocket of drug resistant RTs by changing its conformation.

the cyanovinyloxy group in TMC278 is able to adapt to changes in the shape of the binding pocket caused by drug resistance mutations, and the binding pocket is flexible and can adapt to changes in inhibitor structure, thereby compensating for drug resistance mutations and allowing TMC278 to retain high activity against HIV-1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new drugs to treat HIV 1 infections, and we have developed a new NNRTI (TMC278) that is active against drug resistant HIV  1.
the development of novel non-nucleoside reverse-transcriptase (NNRTI), inhibitors of HIV-1 reverse transcriptase (RT).
the development of a new generation of antiviral agents that can be used to treat HIV infections in the face of drug resistance.

The main takeaway from our work is that

the cyanovinyloxy group of TMC-278 is positioned in the middle of a tunnel between the NNRTI-binding pocket and the nucleic acid-binding cleft, and that the flexibility of the drug is key to its ability to bind wild-type and drug-resistant forms of RT.

the cyanovinyloxy group of TMC-278 is positioned in the hydrophobic tunnel, which connects the NNRTI-binding pocket to the nucleotide-binding cleft of RT, and this group is able to adapt to the shape of the tunnel, which is changed by the mutations.
